stages.title: Aerodynamic coefficients
stages.hook: Engineers test a small model wing in a wind tunnel and then predict the lift of a full-size wing. How can results from a small model apply to a big aircraft?
explain: Instead of quoting forces directly, engineers divide them by a reference: the dynamic pressure q = ½ρv² multiplied by a reference area S. The lift coefficient is C_L = L ÷ (q S), and the drag coefficient is C_D = D ÷ (q S). These numbers have no units, so they describe the shape and angle of the wing, not the size or the speed.

The coefficients let a model result be scaled to the real aircraft, as long as the flows are similar (for example, similar Reynolds number and Mach number). The ratio L/D = C_L ÷ C_D measures aerodynamic efficiency: a glider may reach 30 or more, and a typical airliner is in the region of 15 to 20.

C_L rises roughly in proportion to angle of attack until the airflow begins to separate from the upper surface. After that C_L falls: this is the stall. A drag polar plots C_L against C_D and shows how the two are related.

example.q: A wing of area 16 m² flies at 50 m/s at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) and makes 19 600 N of lift. Find C_L.

analogies.city: Fuel use is quoted in litres per 100 km so cars of different sizes and trips can be compared. Coefficients do the same for wings.
analogies.sport: A batting average divides hits by chances, so players with different numbers of games can be compared.
analogies.home: A recipe scales by ratio, not by quantity: the proportions stay the same when you cook more.
analogies.tech: A scale model of a car in a wind tunnel can predict the full-size car if the flow is matched.

stages.mnemonic: Force over q S: lift gives C_L, drag gives C_D, and L/D tells how smooth the flight.
terms: q = ½ρv², the pressure of the moving flow.
A graph relating C_L and C_D.

misc.wrong: A wing has one fixed lift coefficient.
misc.right: C_L changes with angle of attack, flap setting, Reynolds number and Mach number, and it falls after the stall.

stages.limits: Model tests only match the real aircraft if the flow is dynamically similar. Differences in Reynolds number or compressibility can make coefficients differ.

questions.model: Coefficients remove the effects of size and speed by dividing forces by qS. If the flow is similar, the same coefficient applies to the full-size wing, so force = coefficient × q × S for the real values.
questions.why: Coefficients are dimensionless and transfer between sizes when the flow is similar.

panel.model: At the speed for maximum L/D, drag is smallest for the lift needed, so each metre of height lost gives the greatest forward distance. Glide distance equals height times L/D.
panel.why: Glide ratio equals L/D.

teach.topic: What a lift coefficient tells us
teach.model: A lift coefficient is lift divided by dynamic pressure and wing area. It has no units, so it describes the shape and tilt of the wing, not its size or speed. Engineers use it to predict a real wing from a model.

stages.title: Subsonic airflow
stages.hook: When a river narrows, the water speeds up. Does air do the same when it flows past a wing or through a narrowing duct?
explain: Subsonic means slower than the speed of sound. At sea level in standard air the speed of sound is about 340 m/s. Mach number M = v ÷ a, where a is the speed of sound. For low speeds (below about M 0.3) air density hardly changes, so the flow is treated as incompressible.

For incompressible flow, mass is conserved: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ (continuity). A narrower passage means faster flow. Bernoulli's equation says that along a streamline in steady, inviscid flow, p + ½ρv² stays constant. Faster flow therefore goes with lower pressure.

Bernoulli's principle links speed and pressure but is not a full explanation of lift on its own; the flow is shaped by the wing turning the air. Real air also has viscosity, so a thin boundary layer forms next to the surface.

example.q: Air (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) flows at 20 m/s through a duct of area 0.5 m² into a section of area 0.25 m². Find the speed and the pressure drop (Bernoulli).

analogies.sea: A river speeds up through a narrow gorge.
analogies.home: Put your thumb over the end of a garden hose and the water shoots out faster.
analogies.city: Traffic funnelled into one lane has to move forward at a higher rate to keep the same flow.
analogies.nature: Wind speeds up between two tall buildings or mountains.

stages.mnemonic: Narrow means fast; fast means low pressure (along a streamline).

stages.limits: Bernoulli's equation as written assumes steady, inviscid, incompressible flow. At higher Mach numbers, compressibility must be included.

panel.q: Why can Bernoulli's equation not be applied directly across the boundary layer to the surface of a wing?
panel.model: Bernoulli assumes inviscid flow with no energy loss. Close to the surface viscosity slows the air to zero speed at the wall and dissipates energy, so the equation does not hold along streamlines inside the boundary layer.
panel.why: Viscosity is neglected in Bernoulli's equation.

stages.title: Airfoil pressure distribution
stages.hook: If you could put tiny pressure gauges all around a wing, where would the pressure be lowest, and what would that do?
explain: The pressure on an airfoil is different at every point on its surface. We usually write it as a pressure coefficient C_p = (p − p∞) ÷ q∞, where p∞ is the free-stream pressure and q∞ = ½ρv∞². For incompressible flow, C_p = 1 − (v ÷ v∞)², with v the local speed at the surface.

At the stagnation point v = 0, so C_p = 1, the highest value. Where the air is faster than the free stream, C_p is negative: the pressure is below ambient. On a lifting airfoil the upper surface has strongly negative C_p near the leading edge (suction), and the lower surface has C_p close to zero or positive. The area between the two curves gives the lift.

The net force is found by adding up pressure times area all over the surface. Because pressure acts at right angles to the surface, the net force on a tilted wing has a part at right angles to the free stream (lift) and a part along it (pressure drag). The pressure also gives a pitching moment about the wing.

example.q: Air passes a point on an airfoil at 1.2 times the free-stream speed. Find C_p there, and the pressure difference from ambient if v∞ = 60 m/s, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³.

panel.q: Why is the area between the upper and lower C_p curves a measure of lift?
panel.model: The C_p difference between lower and upper surface is the net pressure pushing up at each point. Adding this over the chord (the area between the curves) gives the net force per unit span, which is the lift to a good approximation.
panel.why: Lift coefficient ≈ integral of (C_p,lower − C_p,upper) along the chord, for small angles.

teach.topic: How the pressure around a wing gives lift
teach.model: Air moves faster over the top of a lifting wing, so the pressure there is lower than ambient. Underneath, the pressure is closer to ambient or higher. Pressure pushes at right angles to the surface, and the sum of the differences gives an upward force.

stages.title: Aircraft performance
stages.hook: Why can a small aircraft take off from a short grass strip but a heavy airliner needs a long runway?
explain: Performance describes what an aircraft can do: how fast, how high, how far, and how steeply it can climb. In level flight lift equals weight, so L = ½ρv²SC_L = W. Solving for speed gives v = √(2W ÷ (ρ S C_L)). The lowest speed that can be flown is the stall speed, found by using the maximum lift coefficient C_L,max: v_s = √(2W ÷ (ρ S C_L,max)).

Heavier aircraft, thinner air (high or hot airfields) and smaller wing area all raise the stall speed. Flaps raise C_L,max so landing and take-off speeds are lower. Take-off and landing distances are longer if the speeds are higher.

Range and endurance depend on engine fuel use and on L/D. In still air, a glider with glide ratio L/D going down a height h can travel a distance about h × (L/D). Airliners cruise high where thin air gives lower drag at high speed.

example.q: A 1000 kg aircraft has S = 16 m² and C_L,max = 1.6. Find its stall speed at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²).

analogies.sport: A heavier sprinter needs a longer run to reach take-off speed in the long jump.
analogies.city: A loaded truck takes longer to reach speed than an empty one.
analogies.farm: A tractor with a heavier load needs a longer start to get going.
analogies.sea: A loaded cargo ship needs a longer distance to stop.

misc.wrong: A plane stalls only when its engine stops.
misc.right: A stall is when the wing's angle of attack is too high and airflow separates. It can happen at any speed or power setting, though it is most likely at low speed.

stages.limits: These are simple formulas for steady flight in still air. Real performance includes engine limits, weather, runway slope and safety margins. The game is educational, not pilot training.

stages.title: Flight mechanics
stages.hook: Climbing needs power, turning tilts the lift, and diving can be exciting. How can we describe all of these using the same four forces?
explain: Flight mechanics applies Newton's laws to aircraft. In a steady climb at angle γ, the forces along the flight path are thrust, drag and the component of weight W sin γ. The rate of climb is the vertical speed: for small angles, ROC ≈ (T − D) v ÷ W, which means excess power divided by weight.

In a steady, level, banked turn at bank angle φ, the vertical component of lift balances weight: L cos φ = W, so L = W ÷ cos φ. The load factor n = L ÷ W = 1 ÷ cos φ, and at 60° bank n = 2, a 'two g' turn. The horizontal component L sin φ gives the centripetal force, so the turn radius is R = v² ÷ (g tan φ).

Because load factor rises quickly at steep banks, stall speed also rises in a turn, by a factor √n. These simple equations assume steady motion and a straight horizontal or nearly horizontal path, and they are the basis for performance charts.

example.q: An aircraft in level flight at 50 m/s banks at 45° in a steady level turn. Find the turn radius (g = 9.81 m/s²).

panel.q: Explain why a climbing aircraft needs more thrust than drag, using forces.
panel.model: When climbing, part of the weight acts backward along the flight path. Thrust must overcome both drag and that component of weight, so thrust has to be greater than drag.

teach.model: In a bank the lift is tilted. The upward part must still hold up the weight, and the sideways part pulls the plane round the turn. So the total lift has to be larger than the weight, and the steeper the bank, the larger it must be.

stages.title: Aircraft structural components
stages.hook: A wing has to hold a whole aircraft up in the air, yet it is thin and light. How is it built so it does not snap?
explain: An aircraft's skeleton is called the airframe. The fuselage carries people and cargo and is built from rings called frames and long strips called stringers, covered by a thin skin. The wing has long beams called spars, running from root to tip, and ribs, which give the airfoil shape and support the skin.

Loads come from lift, weight, the engines and gusts. Stress is force per area: σ = F ÷ A, in pascals. A structure must carry its design loads with a safety margin. Aircraft are designed for a limit load factor (for example 2.5 g for many transport aircraft) and are checked for a larger ultimate load.

Materials need high strength for little mass. Many aircraft use aluminium alloys, and newer ones use composites such as carbon fibre in plastic, which are strong and light. Cycles of loading can cause fatigue cracks, so aircraft are inspected regularly. Cabins are pressurised, which adds a load on the fuselage.

example.q: A rod carries a 50 kN pull and has a cross-section of 0.0005 m². What is the stress?

analogies.city: A bridge has main beams (spars) and cross-supports (ribs) like a wing.
analogies.nature: A bird's bones are hollow and light but strong.
analogies.home: A cardboard tube is stiff for its weight, like a fuselage skin on frames.

A cross piece that gives the wing its airfoil shape.
A long stiffener along the fuselage or wing skin.
Force divided by area, in pascals.

misc.wrong: A stronger material is always the best choice for aircraft.
misc.right: Aircraft need a high ratio of strength to mass, not strength alone. A very strong but heavy material wastes fuel.

questions.why: Spars are the main beams of a wing.

questions.q: What gives a wing its airfoil shape from the inside?
questions.why: Ribs set the cross-section shape and support the skin.

o: They are cheaper than steel in all cases
questions.why: Composites give high strength-to-weight and stiffness-to-weight.

questions.q: Why are aircraft inspected for tiny cracks regularly?
o: Fatigue cracks can grow under repeated loads
Cracks are only there as a kind of decoration
Paint hides every crack so none can form
Wings are made of glass and break easily
questions.why: Repeated loading can start and grow cracks, so inspections find them early.

questions.q: A hollow tube is nearly as stiff in bending as a solid rod of the same outer size, but much lighter. Why?
o: Material far from the centre does most of the resisting
Air inside the tube carries most of the load
Hollow tubes are always stronger than solid rods
Mass does not matter in aircraft design at all
questions.why: Bending stiffness depends mostly on material placed far from the neutral axis.

questions.q: Put these in order from the outside of a fuselage to the inside.
questions.why: The skin is outermost, supported by stringers and frames, and the cabin is inside.

questions.q: Why does a pressurised cabin put extra load on the fuselage?
questions.model: The air pressure inside the cabin is higher than the thin air outside, so it pushes outward on the skin like a balloon. The fuselage must carry this extra stress, and pressurising and depressurising each flight repeats the loading.
questions.why: Pressure difference acts across the skin area and loads the frames.

questions.q: Match each part to its job.
pairs: Gives the fuselage its cross-section shape
questions.why: These are the main parts of the airframe.

panel.q: If the force on a rod stays the same but its cross-section area is halved, the stress
panel.why: σ = F/A, so halving A doubles σ.

panel.q: Why do designers apply a safety factor, such as 1.5, between limit and ultimate load?
o: To allow for uncertainty and damage
To make the aircraft heavier on purpose
Because the law of physics says so
panel.why: Safety margins cover errors in loads, material variation and damage.

panel.q: Why does reducing the mass of the structure matter for an aircraft?
panel.model: Less structural mass means less weight to lift, so the aircraft uses less fuel or can carry more passengers and cargo for the same lift.
panel.why: Weight is a direct cost in lift and fuel.

teach.model: A wing has strong beams called spars that run along its length. Ribs across them give it the airfoil shape, and a thin skin covers the frame. Stress is the force on each unit of area, and designers keep it below what the material can take.

What gives it its shape?
What is stress?

stages.title: Jet engine fundamentals
stages.hook: A jet engine takes in air at the front and throws out a roaring stream at the back. What happens in between to make that stream so much faster?
explain: A gas turbine (turbojet) works in four steps: intake, compression, combustion and exhaust. A compressor squeezes the air, fuel is burned in a combustor, and the hot gas expands through a turbine that drives the compressor, then leaves through a nozzle. The gas leaves faster than the air came in.

Thrust is the change in momentum of the air per second: F = ṁ(v_e − v₀), with ṁ the mass flow rate, v_e the exhaust speed and v₀ the speed of the aircraft. A turbofan has a large fan driven by the core, and most of its thrust comes from air that bypasses the core. The bypass ratio compares bypass air to core air.

Bypass air is accelerated by only a little, which is more efficient at airliner speeds and quieter. Pure turbojets suit very high speeds. Engines lose power at height because thin air carries less mass flow, so thrust falls as altitude rises.

example.q: An engine takes in 100 kg of air per second and the exhaust leaves at 500 m/s relative to an aircraft flying at 250 m/s. Ignoring the added fuel mass, find the thrust.

analogies.sea: A water jet-ski sucks water in and shoots it out of the back faster.
analogies.home: A hairdryer takes in air and blows it out faster and hotter.
analogies.sport: A sprinter pushes off the blocks with a big push backward on the ground.
analogies.tech: A bicycle pump compresses air in the same way a compressor does.

terms: Squeezes the incoming air to a higher pressure.
The chamber where fuel burns in the compressed air.
Wheel turned by the hot gas, driving the compressor and fan.
Mass flow of bypass air divided by core air.
The exit that speeds up the exhaust jet.

misc.wrong: A jet engine pushes against the air behind it.
misc.right: Thrust is the reaction to speeding up air through the engine. It works by changing the momentum of the air, not by pushing against outside air.

stages.limits: The thrust formula ignores the added fuel mass and pressure thrust at the nozzle. Real engines are far more complex, with many compressor and turbine stages.

trip.prompt: Find the labelled diagram. Where is the high-pressure compressor, and where is the combustor?

questions.q: In which order does air pass through a basic jet engine?
questions.why: The air is compressed, heated by burning, expanded through a turbine and then exhausted.

questions.q: An engine passes 100 kg/s of air. The exhaust leaves at 500 m/s relative to the engine and the aircraft flies at 250 m/s. Ignoring fuel mass, what is the thrust in newtons?
A turbofan has a core mass flow of 20 kg/s and a bypass mass flow of 120 kg/s. What is its bypass ratio?
questions.why: Bypass ratio = 120 ÷ 20 = 6.

questions.q: What drives the compressor in a jet engine?
o: The turbine, driven by hot gas
A battery carried inside the engine
The landing gear as it retracts
questions.why: The turbine takes energy from the hot gas and turns a shaft connected to the compressor.

questions.q: Why does a turbofan suit airliners better than a pure turbojet?
o: It moves more air by a smaller speed change, which is more efficient and quieter
It burns no fuel at all while it cruises along
It weighs nothing compared with a turbojet
It makes no thrust from its core, only from the fan, which saves fuel
questions.why: Large bypass flow gives thrust with less wasted kinetic energy in the jet.

questions.q: Why does engine thrust fall as altitude increases?
o: Thinner air means less mass flow through the engine
Gravity gets stronger as the aircraft climbs
The fuel becomes heavy in the cold
The nozzle shrinks as the air cools
questions.why: Thrust depends on mass flow, which falls with air density.

questions.q: Why does a jet engine not work in space?
o: It needs atmospheric air to burn its fuel
It is too small to work outside the atmosphere
Space is too hot for the engine to survive
It needs a supply of water to run
questions.why: Jet engines take oxygen from the air. Rockets carry their own oxidiser.

questions.q: Put these energy conversions in the order they happen in a gas turbine.
items: Fuel burns and heats the gas
Gas leaves as a fast jet
questions.why: Compression, heating, expansion and then exhaust is the Brayton cycle sequence.

questions.q: Explain, using momentum, how a jet engine produces thrust.
questions.model: The engine takes in air and accelerates it so it leaves faster than it came in. The change in momentum of the air per second equals the force on it, and the reaction pushes the engine forward.
questions.why: Thrust is the rate of change of momentum of the air.

questions.q: Match each engine part to its job.
questions.why: These parts form the core of a gas turbine.

panel.q: Two engines give the same thrust. Engine A throws 200 kg/s of air with a 50 m/s speed increase; engine B throws 50 kg/s with 200 m/s. Which wastes less kinetic energy in the jet?
panel.why: Both give 10 000 N, but kinetic energy added is ½ṁΔv², which is smaller with a small Δv and big ṁ.

panel.q: A jet flies faster, so v₀ increases while v_e and ṁ stay the same. The thrust
panel.why: F = ṁ(v_e − v₀); a larger v₀ gives a smaller difference.

panel.q: Why can a jet engine's thrust be changed by adding more fuel without changing air flow?
panel.model: Burning more fuel heats the gas more, so it expands through the turbine and nozzle with more energy and leaves the nozzle faster. A bigger exhaust speed gives a larger thrust.
panel.why: Extra heat raises the exhaust speed v_e.

teach.topic: How a jet engine makes thrust
teach.model: A jet engine sucks in air, squeezes it, burns fuel in it and lets the hot gas rush out of the back. The gas leaves faster than the air came in, so the engine pushes it back and the gas pushes the engine forward.

points.ask: Where does the air come from?

What do we add?

stages.title: Helicopter rotor aerodynamics
stages.hook: A helicopter blade moves forward on one side and backward on the other when the helicopter flies ahead. Why doesn't it roll over?
explain: Each rotor blade is a small wing. As it spins, it makes lift, and the sum of the lift from all blades gives rotor thrust. In a hover, thrust equals weight: T = W. The rotor disk area is A = πR², and disk loading is T ÷ A. A larger rotor spreads the push over more air, which needs less power.

In hover the rotor accelerates air downward. A simple momentum model gives the induced velocity v_i = √(T ÷ (2ρA)). The torque from the rotor turns the helicopter body the other way, so a tail rotor (or another main rotor) provides a balancing torque.

When flying forward, the advancing blade moves through air at speed Ωr plus the aircraft speed, and the retreating blade at Ωr minus it. This would make the advancing side lift far more. Blades flap up on the advancing side and down on the retreating side, which changes their angle of attack and balances the lift. This is called dissymmetry of lift and is a key limit on a helicopter's top speed.

example.q: A helicopter of mass 1200 kg hovers with a rotor of radius 5 m. Find the disk loading (g = 9.81 m/s²).

analogies.home: A ceiling fan pushes air down; a helicopter rotor does it with enough force to lift.
analogies.sea: A propeller on a boat pushes water; a rotor pushes air.
analogies.sport: A rower on one side of a boat would turn it, so rowers balance each side. A tail rotor balances torque.
analogies.nature: A hovering hummingbird pushes air down to stay in place.

stages.mnemonic: Thrust equals weight in a hover; air goes down so the helicopter stays up.
terms: Rotor thrust divided by rotor disk area.
The downward speed given to the air through the rotor.
The blade moving in the same direction as the helicopter's flight.
Unequal lift between advancing and retreating sides.
A small rotor that stops the body from spinning.

misc.wrong: A helicopter hovers because its rotor blades lift it like a fan holding it up in a vacuum.
misc.right: The rotor throws a stream of air downward, and the reaction holds the helicopter up. It cannot hover without air.

stages.limits: The momentum model gives only the ideal minimum power. Real rotors need more power for friction on the blades and other losses. The game is educational, not pilot training.

A rotor has radius 5 m. What is its disk area in m²? Use π = 3.1416.
The helicopter needs 11 772 N of thrust and the disk area is 78.54 m². What is the disk loading in N/m²?

Why does a helicopter with a single main rotor need a tail rotor?
o: To cancel the torque that would spin the body
To make extra lift for the rotor
To cool the engine in the hover
To make the helicopter look balanced
questions.why: The rotor turning one way twists the body the other way.

questions.q: When a helicopter flies forward, which blade meets the faster air?
questions.why: The advancing blade's speed is Ωr plus the aircraft speed.

questions.q: Why does a helicopter with a larger rotor need less power to hover?
o: It accelerates a larger mass of air by a smaller speed
It weighs much less than a small rotor
The air near a large rotor is heavier
Larger rotors spin backward in the hover
questions.why: For the same thrust, a bigger disk gives lower induced velocity and wastes less kinetic energy.

questions.q: Which factor limits the top speed of a conventional helicopter?
o: Dissymmetry of lift and retreating-blade stall
The colour of the tail and body of the helicopter
The length of the runway it uses
The noise made by the engine while it flies
questions.why: At high forward speeds the retreating blade sees too little airspeed and stalls.

questions.q: Two helicopters of equal mass have rotor radii of 3 m and 8 m. Which has the higher disk loading?
questions.why: Disk loading is T/(πR²), which is larger for a smaller disk.

questions.q: Why would a helicopter be unable to hover on the Moon using its rotor?
questions.model: There is almost no atmosphere on the Moon. A rotor works by pushing air down, so with no air there is no reaction force to hold the helicopter up.
questions.why: Rotors need air to push.

panel.q: If the rotor thrust is doubled in a hover with the same rotor, the induced velocity changes by a factor of
panel.why: v_i ∝ √T.

panel.q: A rescue helicopter hovers at a high mountain where the air is thin. What happens to power needed?
o: It rises, because the rotor must move more air faster
It falls to zero, since thin air needs no effort
It stays the same at any height
It is not related to air density at all
panel.why: v_i = √(T/2ρA) rises when ρ falls, and ideal power T v_i rises too.

panel.q: Explain how blade flapping helps a helicopter in forward flight.
panel.model: The advancing blade meets faster air and tends to make more lift, so it flaps upward. This reduces its angle of attack and lift, while the retreating blade flaps down to increase its angle, so the lift on both sides is balanced.
panel.why: Flapping equalises lift between advancing and retreating sides.

teach.model: A helicopter's blades are spinning wings. They push a column of air downward, and the reaction holds the helicopter up. To hover, the upward thrust must equal the weight. A tail rotor stops the body from spinning the other way.

What do they do to the air?

stages.title: Satellite orbit fundamentals
stages.hook: The International Space Station travels at about 7.7 km/s, so a trip around Earth takes only about 90 minutes. Why that speed, and not faster or slower?
explain: A satellite in a circular orbit is in free fall around the planet. Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm ÷ r² = mv² ÷ r. Cancelling m gives the orbital speed v = √(GM ÷ r). For Earth, GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s². Here r is measured from Earth's centre, not the surface (Earth's mean radius is 6371 km).

A larger orbit means lower speed and a longer period. The period is T = 2πr ÷ v. A low orbit at 400 km altitude has r = 6771 km, giving v ≈ 7.67 km/s and T ≈ 92 minutes. A geostationary orbit has a period matching Earth's rotation (about 23 h 56 min) at radius about 42 164 km, about 35 786 km above the equator, and appears fixed in the sky.

The orbit does not depend on the satellite's mass. Moving into a higher orbit takes energy, but the satellite then travels more slowly. Drag from the thin upper atmosphere slowly lowers very low orbits, so such satellites need occasional boosts.

example.q: Find the orbital speed at 400 km altitude. (GM = 3.986×10¹⁴ m³/s²; Earth radius 6371 km.)

analogies.sport: A hammer thrower whirls the hammer on a rope; the rope pulls inward like gravity.
analogies.sea: Swinging a bucket on a rope in a circle: the rope's pull keeps it on the path.
analogies.home: A ball on a string being whirled overhead is like a satellite on gravity's string.
analogies.tech: Navigation satellites are in high orbits so many can be seen from the ground.

stages.mnemonic: Higher means slower and longer: v = √(GM/r).
terms: The speed for a circular orbit: v = √(GM/r).
The time for one full orbit: T = 2πr/v.
An orbit a few hundred kilometres above the surface.
An orbit with a 24-hour (sidereal) period above the equator.

misc.wrong: Satellites in orbit are beyond Earth's gravity.
misc.right: Gravity at the ISS is still about 90% of its value on the ground. Satellites orbit because they fall around Earth while moving sideways fast.

stages.limits: This level treats circular orbits around a spherical Earth with no air drag. Real orbits are slightly elliptical and are disturbed by Earth's shape, the Moon and the Sun.

trip.prompt: Find the range of heights for low Earth orbit. Where is the International Space Station?

questions.q: Use GM = 3.986×10¹⁴ m³/s² and r = 6.771×10⁶ m. What is the circular orbital speed v = √(GM/r) in m/s?
A satellite moves at 7673 m/s on a circle of radius 6.771×10⁶ m. Use T = 2πr/v. What is the period in seconds? (2π = 6.2832)
A satellite orbits at 6371 km (Earth's radius) plus 600 km altitude. What is its orbit radius r from Earth's centre in km?
What provides the centripetal force on a satellite?
questions.why: Gravity pulls the satellite toward the centre of its orbit.

questions.q: Does a satellite's orbital speed at a given radius depend on its mass?
questions.why: Mass cancels in GMm/r² = mv²/r.

questions.q: A satellite moves to a higher circular orbit. What happens to its speed?
questions.why: v = √(GM/r), so larger r gives lower v.

questions.q: Why does a geostationary satellite appear fixed in the sky?
o: Its orbital period matches Earth's rotation and it orbits above the equator
It has no gravity acting on it at that height
It never moves at all, even compared with space
It is held up by a very long cable from the ground
questions.why: It completes one orbit in the time Earth completes one turn, so it stays above the same point.

questions.q: A very low satellite slowly loses height. What is the main cause?
o: Drag from the thin upper atmosphere
The Moon switching off its pull on it
Magnetism between the satellite and Earth
Light pressure from the stars only
questions.why: Even thin air removes energy, so the orbit shrinks over time.

questions.q: Put these orbits in order from the shortest period to the longest.
questions.why: Period increases with orbit radius: about 1.5 h, 12 h, 24 h, 27 days.

questions.q: Explain why astronauts on the space station float even though gravity is still strong there.
questions.model: The station and the astronauts are both in free fall around Earth. They fall together, so there is no push between them and the floor, and the astronauts feel weightless even though gravity is still about 90% of its ground value.
questions.why: Weightlessness is free fall, not an absence of gravity.

panel.q: A satellite must move to a faster orbit around Earth by lowering its altitude. What does a lower orbit do to the period?
panel.why: Lower orbit means a smaller radius and a shorter path at higher speed, so the period gets shorter.

panel.q: If a satellite is slowed by firing its rocket backward (retrograde), it
panel.why: Slowing down reduces the orbit height. The satellite then speeds up as it falls to the lower orbit.

panel.q: Why do geostationary satellites need to orbit so far out, about 35 786 km above the equator?
panel.model: The period of an orbit increases with radius. Only at about 42 164 km from Earth's centre does the period equal one sidereal day, so the satellite stays above the same point.
panel.why: T = 2π√(r³/GM) fixes the radius for a 24-hour period.

teach.model: A satellite keeps falling toward Earth, but it moves sideways so fast that the Earth curves away below it. Gravity provides the pull that bends its path into a circle. A higher orbit means a slower speed and a longer trip around.

Why doesn't it hit the ground?
What shape is its path?
